vignette:
Priya is a 67-year-old married South Asian woman who has worked for two decades at a small nonprofit providing legal aid to immigrant families. She came to therapy at her husband's urging, though she herself found it hard to explain why she had finally agreed. Six months earlier, while walking home from a fundraising event in her neighborhood, she was sexually assaulted by a man who had been loitering near the bus stop. She remembered little of the attack itself beyond a sudden pressure on her shoulder and the smell of damp metal from the chain-link fence she was pushed against. What stayed with her most vividly was the moment afterward-sitting alone on a curb in the dark, her skirt torn, her phone dead, and a faint sense that the man had said something she could not make out. She did not call the police. She did not tell anyone at work. She told her husband only that she had tripped and needed new shoes.

In the weeks that followed, Priya returned to her normal routines. She kept taking the same bus to the office, went to the same grocery store, and attended her monthly volunteer meetings at the local temple. Her colleagues noticed nothing unusual. Her husband, a retired accountant, assumed the quietness he saw in her was simply age and tiredness. Yet inside, Priya felt a persistent, leaden unease that she could not name to herself. She began to feel that the assault had changed something fundamental-that the man had seen something in her that she had not known was there, something that made her vulnerable in a way she had never before considered. She started avoiding the bus stop by crossing the street two blocks early, though she told herself it was just a shorter route. She stopped taking evening walks altogether, saying her knees hurt.

At work, her sense of purpose began to fray. She had always been the person clients trusted, the one who listened without judgment. Now she found herself rushing through intake interviews, her eyes fixed on the clock, her mind skidding away from stories that involved physical danger. She missed a deadline for the first time in twenty years and blamed it on a faulty computer. Her supervisor, a younger woman Priya had mentored, asked gently if something was wrong. Priya shook her head and said she was fine. She was certain that if she admitted to having been assaulted, people would see her differently-would see her as someone who had allowed it to happen, or who was now too fragile to do her job. That conviction grew stronger each week, even as the distance from the event stretched. She became more guarded with her husband, less sure of his steady kindness, and started sleeping in the guest room because she could not bear the weight of his hand on her shoulder at night.

What finally brought Priya to the clinic was not an acute crisis but a cumulative exhaustion. She had begun to suspect that the attack had not ended that night-that it was still happening, repeating inside her in a loop she could not stop or slow down. She did not want to name the images that came unbidden; she only knew that by the time she sat in the waiting room, she had been crying without reason for three days. When the therapist asked what she hoped for, Priya paused a long time. She said she wanted to feel like her own person again-like the woman who had taken charge of a nonprofit food drive, who had raised two children, who had never once doubted that the world made sense. She also said, quietly, that she was afraid that asking for help might prove she had been weak all along. That fear sat in the room with her, unlabelled, as she waited to see if anyone could hear it and not turn away.
